meta.title: Who really said "Life is really simple, but we insist on making it complicated"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Confucius never said it. This tidy line isn’t in the Analects; its earliest print trace is a 1949 magazine, author unknown.

meta.ogDescription: Not Confucius. The line appears in no classical Chinese text; Wikiquote traces its earliest print to 1949, with no known author.

answer.label: Not Confucius — a modern saying wrongly pinned on him
answer.authorDates: Confucius: 551–479 BC · the real wording has no known author
answer.sourceLine: This line appears nowhere in the Analects or any classical Chinese text. Wikiquote’s editors file it under “Misattributed — Not Chinese,” noting it was “attributed on the internet but not found in print prior to an attribution in Aero Digest, Vols. 58–59, 1949.” Its true originator is unknown.

source.heading: The source trail
source.excerpt: Life is really simple, but we insist on making it complicated.
trail: Wikiquote’s Confucius page files the exact line under Misattributed — Not Chinese, noting it was “not found in print prior to an attribution in Aero Digest, Vols. 58–59, 1949.”
The wording appears in none of the sayings that make up the Analects of Confucius, the primary record of his teaching.
Quote aggregators such as Goodreads and BrainyQuote repeat the Confucius credit with no source, which is how the misattribution spreads.
source.excerptNote: Widely captioned as Confucius, but absent from every classical Confucian text. A common variant reads “…but men insist on making it complicated.”
source.rightsNote: The wording’s origin is unknown: it is not tied to any identifiable author or datable work, and its earliest documented print appearance is a 1949 magazine citation. Because we cannot attach it to a specific published source, no public-domain claim can be made honestly.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Who it’s pinned on
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese philosopher & teacher, subject of the Analects
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu) was a Chinese philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period whose ethics of virtue, ritual, and social harmony shaped East Asian thought for millennia. His teachings survive chiefly in the Analects, a collection of sayings compiled by his followers after his death. Because his name signals ancient wisdom, it has become one of the internet’s favorite magnets for tidy modern aphorisms he never uttered — this line among them.

cite.sourceCitation: “Confucius (Misattributed — Not Chinese),” Wikiquote, noting earliest print in Aero Digest, Vols. 58–59 (1949), p. 115. No classical Confucian source contains the line.

copyAttribution: Unknown author, popularly (and wrongly) attributed to Confucius. The line appears in no classical Chinese text; its earliest known print trace is Aero Digest (1949).

misattribution.heading: How Confucius got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of countless feel-good aphorisms attached to Confucius because his name lends instant, ancient authority. It has no basis in his actual work.

items.why: The sentence appears in none of the classical Confucian texts. Wikiquote catalogues it under “Misattributed — Not Chinese”, reporting that it was “not found in print prior to an attribution in Aero Digest, Vols. 58–59, 1949.”
A widely shared alternate form swaps in “but men insist on making it complicated.” Both versions circulate under Confucius’s name; neither is traceable to him.

misattribution.truthLine: Confucius almost certainly never said this. The wording surfaces in no classical Chinese source, and its earliest print trace — per Wikiquote — is a 1949 magazine, with no known original author.

context.heading: Why this keeps getting pinned on Confucius
lead: Confucius is a magnet for modern aphorisms for the same reason as Einstein, Twain, and Gandhi: attaching a name that means “timeless wisdom” makes a tidy line feel weightier and stops readers asking where it came from. A crisp paradox about simplicity fits the popular image of a sage, so few pause to check whether it is actually in the Analects.

The honest answer is that no one knows who first wrote it. The trail goes cold at a 1949 trade magazine, and even there it is a floating aphorism rather than a sourced Confucian saying. That absence — not a rival author — is the whole story.
context.pull: A name that means “ancient wisdom” is exactly what a rootless quote needs to survive.
